subject: physics
question_text: Can a vector of magnitude zero have non-zero components?

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), VERY SHORT ANSWER 6 of Unit 4. The mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed for Unit 4, so appearances[] stays empty.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The reason
lines: No. For a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k the
Squares are never negative, so the sum
is zero only if every term is zero.
steps.margin_note: The reason IS the mark: squares cannot cancel each other, so nothing can hide.
steps.why: One non-zero component contributes a positive square that nothing else can cancel — so a zero magnitude forces every component to be zero.
common_mistakes: Answering yes, imagining components that cancel — they add as squares, not as signed numbers.

recall.must_convey: That the magnitude is the root of the sum of squares, and squares cannot cancel.
accept: sum of squares is zero only if each is zero
root of a one square plus a two square

steps.memory_tip: Try a = 3i − 3j: |a| = √(9 + 9) = √18, not 0. The minus sign disappears in the square.

steps.label: The conclusion
steps.margin_note: State the conclusion as the boxed line: every component must be zero.
steps.why: This is why the null vector is unique: there is exactly one way to have zero length.
common_mistakes: Boxing only "No" without the component statement.

recall.must_convey: That every component must be zero — a zero-magnitude vector cannot have non-zero components.

steps.memory_tip: Read it backwards as well: zero magnitude and all components zero say the same thing.

insider_note: The word No carries no mark on its own. One mark is the square-root reason, the other is stating that all three components are zero.
